specAnchors.text: understand how ions are formed by electron loss or gain

primer.text: Atomic structure is old ground: protons and electrons counted, shells filled two-eight-eight. This note puts that picture to work - when atoms give up or take in electrons to reach a full outer shell, the balance between protons and electrons tips and charged particles called ions appear.

modules.title: Formation of Ions
modules.opening: When an atom loses or gains electrons it stops being neutral and becomes an ion - a charged particle. Atoms make this trade to reach a full outer shell, the stable arrangement the noble gases already hold. Lose electrons and the charge is positive; gain them and it is negative.
keyPoints: An ion is an atom or group of atoms that carries an electric charge after losing or gaining electrons.
The loss or gain of electrons happens so the atom can reach a full outer shell.
Ions of group 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 elements end with a noble gas electronic structure.
The noble gases named in the note are helium, neon and argon.
Every metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positive ion; every non-metal gains electrons and becomes a negative ion.

low.restatement: Ions form when atoms give up or take in electrons, and the charge tells which way it went: positive for lost, negative for gained. Groups 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 all land on a noble gas arrangement.
low.analogy: Think of a supermarket loyalty card: a shopper one sticker short of a free item grabs one more, while a shopper holding one too many hands it back. Atoms gain or shed electrons the same way to reach a full card - a full outer shell.
low.examPointer: Exam questions ask why ions carry their charges: the answer is electron loss or gain, never proton changes - the nucleus never moves.

medium.restatement: The definition has two halves: the particle, one atom or a group of atoms, and the charge, set by electrons lost or gained. Reaching a full outer shell is the driver, which is why group membership predicts the charge before any formula work starts.
medium.analogy: A full bus already moving is like a noble gas atom - complete, so it does not bother changing. Atoms short of a full bus squeeze on, atoms with spare passengers step off; either way the journey ends with a complete shell.
medium.examPointer: The note's exam hint is worth memorising: electrons gained or lost equal the charge, so 2 electrons lost means 2+, and 1 electron gained means 1-.

modules.title: Formation of Cations and Anions
modules.opening: Two names sort the charged particles: cations are positive ions born from lost electrons, anions are negative ions built from gained ones. Metals always lose, non-metals always gain. The diagrams trace sodium dropping one electron to become Na+, and chlorine picking one up to become Cl-.
keyPoints: Cations are positive ions that form when atoms lose electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.
Anions are negative ions that form when atoms gain electrons, ending with more electrons than protons.
Every metal sheds electrons to other atoms and turns into a positive ion.
Every non-metal takes electrons from other atoms and turns into a negative ion.
A magnesium atom that loses 2 electrons carries a 2+ charge; a bromine atom that gains 1 electron carries a 1- charge.

low.restatement: Cations and anions are the two names to keep straight: cations lost electrons and read positive, anions gained electrons and read negative. Metals feed one side, non-metals the other, and the note's diagrams show sodium and chlorine each taking their route.
low.analogy: Paying for a bus fare works both ways: hand over coins and you are short, take coins in and you are carrying extra. Electrons are the currency - paying them out charges the ion positive, collecting them charges it negative.
low.examPointer: Charge questions answer themselves once the count is known: magnesium losing 2 electrons reads 2+, bromine gaining 1 electron reads 1-.

medium.restatement: The pairing is symmetrical: a cation has more protons than electrons because electrons left, and an anion has more electrons than protons because electrons arrived. The sodium and chloride diagrams mirror each other - one electron out for the metal, one electron in for the non-metal.
medium.analogy: Two shop tills face each other at closing: one till pays out and its balance runs positive on the ledger of lost coins, the other takes in and runs negative. Metals pay electrons out, non-metals take them in, and the charge records the direction.
medium.examPointer: Diagram questions expect the charge arrow as well as the movement: Na+ and Cl- must carry their signs, and the exam hint's count rule justifies each one.

glossary.definition: An atom or group of atoms that carries an electric charge after losing or gaining electrons.
The complete outermost electron shell that atoms chase when they lose or gain electrons.
One of the unreactive elements with a full outer shell already in place - helium, neon and argon are the named examples.
The arrangement of electrons across an atom's shells.
The sign and size of the imbalance left when electrons are gained or lost, quoted as 1-, 2+ and so on.
A positive ion, formed when an atom loses electrons.
A negative ion, formed when an atom gains electrons.

workedExample.prompt: a) A magnesium atom loses 2 electrons. State the charge of the ion formed and the name for this type of ion. b) A bromine atom gains 1 electron. State the charge and the ion type. c) Explain why ions of Group 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 elements have a noble-gas electronic structure.
steps: a) The number of electrons lost equals the charge, so losing 2 electrons gives a Mg2+ ion — a cation, the name for a positive ion formed by electron loss.
b) Gaining 1 electron gives a 1- charge, so the ion is Br- — an anion, the name for a negative ion formed by electron gain.

c) Atoms lose or gain electrons precisely to obtain a full outer shell, which is the arrangement noble gases such as helium, neon and argon already hold; ions of these groups therefore finish with a noble-gas electronic structure.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Mg2+, a cation. b) Br-, an anion. c) The electron loss or gain happens to reach a full outer shell — the noble-gas configuration.
